A new study may have settled the contentious debate over the efficacy of digital readers versus hard copy books by observing the brain processes behind reading for each format. plan.title: Kindle vs Paper Books: What Science Says
plan.description: Does reading on a Kindle change how much you remember? We compare paper books and e-readers on comprehension, memory and what to pick.

beats.narration: You finish a novel on your Kindle. A week later, can you say what happened first, and what came next? Research suggests the paper reader often can. So which should you choose?

props.alt: woman holding a tablet reader on a sofa

beats.narration: A 2018 meta-analysis of 54 experiments found an advantage for paper. In one Kindle study, readers did equally well on most tests. But on timing and the order of events, print readers did better.

props.verdict: Paper wins on remembering the plot order

beats.narration: Why? Pages give physical cues, like where you are in the book. Screens also invite skimming. Researchers call this the screen inferiority effect: people often remember less from digital text.

props.definition: People often understand and remember less from digital texts than from print.

beats.narration: Still, neither format is dying. Print sells over 750 million copies a year in the US, while ebooks hold roughly a fifth to a quarter of the market by revenue.

props.title: Ebook share of US book revenue, roughly

beats.narration: So decide by purpose. For studying, stories you want to remember, or reading with kids, choose paper. For travel, quick reads, or light fiction, a Kindle is perfectly fine.

hook_close.hook_text: You finish a novel on your Kindle. A week later, can you say what happened first, and what came next? Research suggests the paper reader often can. So which should you choose?
hook_close.close_text: So decide by purpose. For studying, stories you want to remember, or reading with kids, choose paper. For travel, quick reads, or light fiction, a Kindle is perfectly fine.

accuracy.reason: The core claims trace to the notes (Delgado 2018, 54 experiments, 750M+ print units, 20–25% ebook share). But the pie chart plots a 22.5% midpoint invented from a range, and the Kindle study is stretched into a general 'timing' claim.

coverage.reason: The request's checklist items are mostly missing: eye strain, battery, portability detail, price and the environmental angle all go unmentioned. The script is almost entirely about comprehension and market share.

structure.reason: The order is clear: hook, evidence, why, market, advice. But beat 4 (market share) is a tangent that does little for the decision, and the final choice ends up thin.

hook_ending.reason: The opening question about recalling what happened first is a good hook. The ending is a practical rule of thumb rather than an image, which is fine but not memorable.

tone.reason: Conversational and neutral, suited to a general US viewer.

visuals.reason: The scene types vary (clip, versus, definition, pie, checklist). But the pie is built on a made-up midpoint, and the checklist titled 'Pick paper when...' contains a Kindle item that is unchecked, which is confusing.

originality.reason: The order-of-events finding is a fairly specific, non-obvious fact. The rest is generic.

instructions.reason: It is not a fair comparison covering the requested practical factors. It leans toward paper and skips most of the expected dimensions. The length is roughly right.

language.reason: Fluent and clean. The sentence 'Research suggests the paper reader often can' is slightly awkward.

defects.issue: Eye strain, battery, price, the environmental angle and the feel of a book are never discussed, even though the brief calls for a fair comparison across them.
The chart shows false precision: 22.5% is a midpoint of a 20–25% range, and the narration says only 'roughly'.

defects.quote: Pages give physical cues, like where you are in the book.
defects.issue: This is a plausible reading of the notes but is presented as an established cause. The notes only suggest it ('may process').
A Kindle item sits inside a 'Pick paper when...' checklist and is shown unchecked, which muddles the message.
The market-share beat is tangential and takes time away from the comparison factors the viewer cares about.

defects.quote: In one Kindle study, readers did equally well on most tests.
defects.issue: The versus table generalises a single small study into 'Paper wins on remembering the plot order'. The notes say the evidence is mixed.

missing: Eye strain and e-ink vs backlit screens
Portability: one device holds thousands of books
The feel and smell of a book, and sentimental value
A takeaway by reader type framed fairly
wrong_facts: The 22.5% ebook share is an invented midpoint of the notes' 20–25% range.
judge.summary: A tidy, well-hooked script, but it is essentially a comprehension-research piece, skipping eye strain, battery, price, environment and feel. It also tilts toward paper rather than giving the fair comparison requested.
